newsitem.title: FRANCE: French unions fight to rekindle crippling protest.
newsitem.headline: French unions fight to rekindle crippling protest.

text.p: Trade unions will on Friday mark the anniversary of Prime Minister Alain Juppe's unpopular welfare reform plans with strikes and protests, but unrest will be a pale shadow of last year's crippling campaign.

Paris commuters will suffer the brunt of the disruption, with a 24-hour public transport strike called by three trade unions to press demands for jobs, wage increases and improved security to protect staff.
Adding to commuters' woes, news on the protest's impact was scarce on Thursday because journalists staged a second one-day strike against government plans to scrap a 30 percent tax break.
Friday should crown a low-key week of lone protests called by the Communist-led CGT union to demand wage increases, protest against job cuts and urge a halt to privatisation.

The CGT's appeal fell flat, with this week's biggest protest a rail strike which hit traffic in parts of southern France and brought services to northeastern Spain to a standstill. Rail workers are fighting job cuts at the loss-making state railway company SNCF and demand new staff be hired.

Divisions over policy and strategy have taken their toll of union strength since the Gaullist Juppe's announcement of welfare reforms triggered a 24-day wave of strikes that crippled the capital in November-December last year.
The pro-Socialist CFDT, France's biggest union, has refused to take part in Friday's anniversary protest because last year it backed the reforms and stayed on the strike's sidelines.
Also keeping his distance from the rival CGT, Marc Blondel of the non-partisan Force Ouvriere union refused to heed the CGT appeal and called rival anti-government rallies for Saturday.
"Worker unity just for the sake of unity is worthless," Blondel said earlier this month, conceding that "for the moment we don't have the detonator" for any new wave of strikes.

Paris transport management said that Friday's protest was expected to cut traffic on the Metro underground railway and on RER regional express lines by half. Eight in every 10 buses are expected to run.
Pilots' unions at Air France Europe, part of the Air France group, have called a new 48-hour strike on Friday and Saturday to protest at planned job cuts. Unions said all flights risked cancellation.
The approval rating of Juppe, under fire for government austerity policies at a time of persistently high unemployment, fell to a new low in an opinion poll published on Wednesday.

Just 25 percent approved of Juppe's performance in office while 72 percent disapproved in the latest Gallup poll for the weekly L'Express, the least favourable rating since he became prime minister in May 1995.
As journalists went on strike, public broadcasting stations provided only limited news services and many newspapers, especially outside the capital Paris, cancelled Friday editions.
At Agence France Presse (AFP) news agency, French-language services were sending only urgent copy, while international services were unaffected. Reuters' French-language services were also affected.

But there were signs that fewer journalists took part in the protest compared with a similar walkout last month. Journalists at several dailies, including Le Monde, Liberation and financial newspapers Les Echos and La Tribune Desfosses, remained at work.

The government plans to scrap a 30 percent income tax deduction for journalists and similar deductions for more than 100 other professions, including airline crews and fashion models, as part of a reform which will reduce income tax for most taxpayers.
